paragraphs: Odysseus and Diomedes go out as spies and meet Dolon, who gives them information. They then kill him, and using what he told them, they kill Rhesus king of the Thracians and take his horses.

All the other princes of the Achaeans slept soundly through the night, but Agamemnon son of Atreus was troubled and could find no rest. The husband of fair Hera sometimes flashes his lightning as a sign of heavy rain, or hail, or a snowfall that turns the ground white, or else as a sign that he will open the wide jaws of hungry war. In the same way Agamemnon heaved many a heavy sigh, for his soul trembled within him. When he looked out over the plain of Troy, he marveled at the many watchfires burning in front of Ilium, and at the sound of pipes and flutes and the hum of men. But when he turned toward the ships and the armies of the Achaeans, he tore his hair out by handfuls before Zeus on high, and groaned aloud, so uneasy was his soul. In the end he decided it was best to go at once to Nestor son of Neleus, and see whether the two of them could find some way to save the Achaeans from destruction. So he got up, put on his shirt, tied his sandals on his comely feet, threw over his shoulders the skin of a huge tawny lion—a skin that reached his feet—and took his spear in his hand.

Menelaus could not sleep either. He too feared disaster for the Argives, who had sailed far over the seas for his sake to fight the Trojans. He draped the skin of a spotted panther over his broad back, set a bronze helmet on his head, and took his spear in his strong hand. Then he went to wake his brother, who was by far the most powerful of the Achaeans and was honored by the people as if he were a god. He found Agamemnon by the stern of his ship, already putting his fine armor on his shoulders, and Agamemnon was very glad that his brother had come.

Menelaus spoke first. “My dear brother,” he said, “why are you arming? Are you going to send one of our comrades to scout the Trojans? I am afraid no one will do you this service, to spy on the enemy alone in the dead of night. It would take great daring.”

King Agamemnon answered, “Menelaus, both of us need shrewd advice to save the Argives and our ships. Zeus has changed his mind, and favors Hector’s sacrifices over ours. I never saw or heard of any one man doing so much damage in a single day as Hector has now done to the sons of the Achaeans—and he did it all by himself, though he is the son of neither god nor goddess. The Argives will regret it long and bitterly. Now run quickly along the line of the ships and call Ajax and Idomeneus. Meanwhile I will go to Nestor and tell him to get up and go among our companies of sentinels to give them their instructions. They will listen to him sooner than to anyone, since his own son and Meriones, the brother in arms of Idomeneus, are the captains over them. It was to those two especially that we gave this charge.”

Menelaus replied, “What exactly do you mean? Should I stay with them and wait for you to come, or come back here once I have delivered your orders?” “Wait there,” King Agamemnon answered, “because there are so many paths through the camp that we might miss each other. Call every man you pass, and tell him to get up. Address him by his family and his father’s name, and give each the full respect due to him. Do not stand on your own dignity. We must take our full share of the work, since Zeus laid this heavy burden on us at our birth.”

With these instructions he sent his brother off, and went on to Nestor, shepherd of his people. He found him asleep in his tent near his own ship. His fine armor lay beside him—his shield, his two spears and his helmet. Beside him also lay the gleaming belt that the old man put on when he armed to lead his people into battle, for age did not hold him back. Nestor raised himself on his elbow and looked up at Agamemnon. “Who is this,” he said, “walking alone through the army and along the ships in the dead of night, while other men are sleeping? Are you looking for one of your mules, or for a comrade? Do not just stand there silent. Speak. What is your business?”

Agamemnon answered, “Nestor, son of Neleus, honor of the Achaean name, it is I, Agamemnon son of Atreus. Zeus has laid labor and sorrow on me for as long as I have breath in my body and my limbs carry me. I am out like this because sleep will not settle on my eyelids. My heart is heavy with the war and with the danger the Achaeans are in. I fear greatly for the Danaans. I am adrift at sea, with no sure counsel; my heart pounds as though it would leap out of my body, and my limbs fail me. So if you can do anything—for you cannot sleep either—let us make the round of the watch and see whether the sentinels are drowsy with toil and sleeping instead of doing their duty. The enemy is camped close by, and for all we know he may attack us by night.”

Nestor replied, “Most noble son of Atreus, Agamemnon, king of men, Zeus will not give Hector everything Hector expects. He will have plenty of troubles yet, if Achilles will put aside his anger. I will go with you, and we will wake others: the son of Tydeus, or Odysseus, or swift Ajax and the valiant son of Phyleus. Someone should also go and call Ajax and King Idomeneus, since their ships are not close at hand but the farthest of all. But I cannot help blaming Menelaus, much as I love and respect him—and I will say so plainly, even at the risk of offending you—for sleeping and leaving all this trouble to you alone. He ought to be going around begging for help from all the princes of the Achaeans, for we are in extreme danger.”

Agamemnon answered, “Sir, you may sometimes blame him justly, for he is often slow and unwilling to exert himself. It is not from laziness or carelessness, but because he looks to me and expects me to take the lead. This time, though, he was awake before I was and came to me of his own accord. I have already sent him to call the very men you named. Now let us go. We will find them with the watch outside the gates, since that is where I said we would meet them.”
“Then,” said Nestor, “no Argive will find fault with him, or ignore his orders, when he calls on them to fight or tells them what to do.”

With this Nestor put on his shirt and tied his sandals on his comely feet. He fastened on his purple coat, which was double-thick, large, and rough and shaggy, took up his formidable bronze-shod spear, and made his way along the line of the Achaean ships. First he called loudly to Odysseus, peer of gods in counsel, and woke him; Odysseus was roused at once by the sound of the battle cry. He came outside his tent and said, “Why are you going alone through the army and along the ships in the stillness of the night? What is so urgent?” Nestor, knight of Gerene, answered, “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, do not take it badly, for the Achaeans are in great trouble. Come with me and let us wake someone else, who can help us decide whether we should fight or flee.”

At this Odysseus went straight into his tent, slung his shield over his shoulders and came out with them. They went first to Diomedes son of Tydeus. They found him outside his tent in full armor, with his comrades sleeping around him and using their shields as pillows. Their spears stood upright on the spikes at their butt ends, driven into the ground, and the burnished bronze flashed far off like the lightning of father Zeus. The hero was sleeping on the skin of an ox, with a piece of fine carpet under his head. Nestor went up to him and nudged him with his heel to wake him, scolding him and urging him to get moving. “Wake up,” he cried, “son of Tydeus. How can you sleep on like this? Do you not see that the Trojans are camped on the brow of the plain close to our ships, with only a little space between us and them?”

At these words Diomedes leaped up and said, “Old man, your heart is iron. You do not rest from your labors for a single moment. Are there no younger men among the Achaeans who could go around and wake the princes? Nothing wears you out.”

Nestor, knight of Gerene, replied, “My son, everything you say is true. I have good sons, and plenty of other men who could call the chieftains. But the Achaeans are in the gravest danger. Life and death hang, as it were, on the edge of a razor. So go, since you are younger than I am, and out of courtesy wake Ajax and the swift son of Phyleus.”

Diomedes threw the skin of a great tawny lion over his shoulders—a skin that reached his feet—and took up his spear. He woke the heroes and brought them back with him. Then they made the round of the men on guard, and found the captains not sleeping at their posts but awake and sitting with their arms about them. As sheep dogs guard their penned flocks and hear a wild beast coming toward them through the mountain forest, and at once dogs and men raise a cry and sleep is broken, so sleep was driven from the eyes of the Achaeans as they kept the watches of that wicked night, for they kept turning toward the plain whenever they heard any stir among the Trojans. The old man was glad and told them to take heart. “Keep watching, my children,” he said, “and do not let sleep take hold of you, or our enemies will triumph over us.”

With this Nestor crossed the trench, and the other chiefs of the Achaeans who had been called to the council went with him. Meriones and the brave son of Nestor went too, because the princes told them to. Beyond the trench that was dug around the wall, they held their meeting on open ground, where there was a clear space free of corpses. It was here that Hector had turned back from his attack on the Argives when night fell. They sat down and talked it over together.

Nestor spoke first. “My friends,” he said, “is any man bold enough to venture among the Trojans, and cut off some straggler, or bring us news of what the enemy mean to do? Will they stay here by the ships, away from the city, or now that they have beaten the Achaeans, will they retire inside their walls? If he could learn all this and come back here safely, his fame would reach as high as heaven in the mouths of all men, and he would be richly rewarded. The chiefs from all our ships would each give him a black ewe with her lamb—a gift of surpassing value—and he would be invited as a guest to all feasts and clan gatherings.”

They all kept silent, but Diomedes of the loud war cry spoke. “Nestor,” he said, “I will gladly go to the army of the Trojans opposite us. But if another man will go with me, I will do it with more confidence and comfort. When two men are together, one of them may notice some opportunity that the other has missed. A man alone is less resourceful, and his wit is weaker.”

At this several men offered to go with Diomedes. The two Ajaxes, servants of Ares, Meriones, and the son of Nestor all wanted to go, and so did Menelaus son of Atreus. Odysseus also wished to go among the army of the Trojans, for he was always full of daring. Then Agamemnon, king of men, spoke. “Diomedes,” he said, “son of Tydeus, man after my own heart, choose your comrade yourself. Take the best man of those who have offered, for many would go with you now. Do not out of delicacy turn down the better man and take the worse out of respect for his birth, because he is of more royal blood.”

Agamemnon said this because he feared for Menelaus. Diomedes answered, “If you tell me to take the man of my own choice, how can I fail to think of Odysseus? No man is more eager to face every kind of danger, and Pallas Athena loves him well. If he went with me, we could pass safely through fire itself, for he is quick to see and understand.”

“Son of Tydeus,” Odysseus replied, “say neither good nor bad about me, for you are among Argives who know me well. Let us go, for the night is waning and dawn is near. The stars have moved on, two-thirds of the night is already gone, and only the third part is left to us.”

Then they put on their armor. Brave Thrasymedes gave the son of Tydeus a sword and a shield (for Diomedes had left his own at his ship), and set a helmet of bull’s hide on his head, without peak or crest. It is called a skull-cap and is a common headgear. Meriones found a bow and quiver for Odysseus, and set on his head a leather helmet. It was lined inside with a strong weaving of leather thongs, and on the outside it was thickly studded with boar’s teeth, skillfully and well set into it; next to the head was an inner lining of felt. Autolycus had stolen this helmet out of Eleon, when he broke into the house of Amyntor son of Ormenus. He gave it to Amphidamas of Cythera to take to Scandea, and Amphidamas gave it as a guest-gift to Molus, who gave it to his son Meriones. Now it was set on the head of Odysseus.

When the pair had armed, they set out and left the other chieftains behind. Pallas Athena sent them a heron by the wayside on their right. They could not see it in the dark, but they heard its cry. Odysseus was glad to hear it and prayed to Athena. “Hear me,” he cried, “daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus. You watch over all my ways and are with me in all my hardships. Be my friend now, in this hour, and grant that we may return to the ships covered with glory, after achieving some mighty exploit that will bring sorrow to the Trojans.”

Then Diomedes of the loud war cry prayed as well. “Hear me too,” he said, “unwearying daughter of Zeus. Be with me as you were with my noble father Tydeus, when he went to Thebes as an envoy sent by the Achaeans. He left the Achaeans by the banks of the river Aesopus and went to the city carrying a message of peace to the Cadmeians. On his way back, with your help, goddess, he did great deeds of daring, for you were his ready helper. In the same way guide me and guard me now, and in return I will sacrifice to you a broad-browed heifer a year old, unbroken, never yet brought under the yoke by any man. I will gild her horns and offer her up to you in sacrifice.”
